idiom_name: hand-written URL-keyed response table (or a shared nginx-style content cache in front)
implementation_notes: C has no page-cache construct, so the classic structure is written by hand or delegated to a C server outside the process. In-process you derive the key from method, path and the headers you vary on, keep the rendered bytes with an ETag and an expiry in a hash table guarded by a pthread_rwlock_t, and serve hits with write()/writev() - or sendfile(2)/mmap(2) for file-backed entries - without running the controller, the queries or the template engine; a miss renders the page, stores the buffer and serves it. In practice most C deployments keep the origin dumb and put shared caching in front of it instead: nginx's proxy_cache/fastcgi_cache or Varnish owns the key zone, TTL, purge and eviction policy, which are exactly the parts that are painful to reimplement. Hand-write the store only when the page is expensive and provably pure with respect to the key.
pitfalls: An unguarded table is an unbounded memory leak: entries need a TTL, a maximum size and an eviction rule, or a hostile query-string space grows the cache until the process dies.

Serving from memory while another thread replaces an entry needs one lock discipline (pthread_rwlock_t, or copy-on-write with a generation counter); handing out a body pointer that is freed underneath the writer is the classic crash.
Building the key with strcat into a fixed buffer truncates long URLs and makes distinct pages collide - use snprintf with the buffer size, and include every axis named in Vary.
Omitting the Vary/authorisation check serves a cached page to the wrong caller: a body computed for one user must never be cached under a key that does not contain that user.
